title: A medical accident took her sight. It didn't take her plan for 200 other people. September 26, 2026.
excerpt: From a reformer who spent his own privilege on someone else's rights to a farming mission built on sharing instead of owning, September 26's five stories share one thread: the biggest gains came from giving something up, not gaining something new.
bodyHtml:
Every story today is really about subtraction - a privilege spent, a founder's own past setbacks, a sense stripped away by accident, ownership given up for access. In each case, giving something up is exactly what made the larger thing possible.

September 26, 1820: the reformer who spent his own privilege on someone else's rights

Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar was born on September 26, 1820, in Birsingha, Bengal, into a family struggling with poverty. He excelled at Sanskrit College, Calcutta, earning the title 'Vidyasagar,' Ocean of Learning. As principal from 1851, he admitted students from lower castes and promoted English study - unusual moves for an orthodox Brahman of his standing. He led the campaign that passed the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act of 1856, opposed child marriage and polygamy, and pushed girls' education, all while refining the Bengali alphabet and writing textbooks still used today.

An Indian fintech founder now runs the app 3 billion people use to talk to each other

On June 22, 2026, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg named Kunal Shah, founder of CRED, as global head of WhatsApp - the first Indian to lead the world's largest messaging platform. Shah co-founded FreeCharge in 2010, sold to Snapdeal in 2015 in what was then India's largest startup acquisition, then founded CRED in 2018, scaling it to 17 million members. His appointment came alongside a Meta-led $900 million investment in CRED itself.

A medical accident took her sight. It didn't take her plan for 200 other people

Tiffany Brar lost her sight as an infant in Chennai due to oxygen toxicity - a medical accident, not a condition she was born with. She studied at the Mary Scott Home for the Blind in Darjeeling before starting the Jyothirgamaya mobile school for the blind in 2012, teaching Braille, computer skills and life skills to over 200 blind people across rural Kerala. In 2022, still her most recent major honor, the President of India awarded her the Nari Shakti Puraskar, the country's highest civilian honor for women.

He studied why India's own town councils don't work. It won him political science's top prize

Shikhar Singh, Assistant Professor of Political Science at Duke University, received the 2026 Heinz I. Eulau Award alongside co-authors Adam Auerbach and Tariq Thachil, for their American Political Science Review article on India's municipal governance. Their fieldwork in India's small-town councils found elected officials often lack the basic procedural knowledge to govern - a factor overlooked in most accountability research. Singh's book 'Migrants and Machine Politics' has separately won four major prizes.

India's plan: one trained drone entrepreneur for every village council

India's '1 Panchayat - 1 Drone Udyami' national mission aims to create 2 lakh trained drone entrepreneurs across 2 lakh agricultural panchayats over five years. Rather than each farmer buying a drone, one trained 'Drone Udyami' runs a shared service centre - spraying, seed broadcasting, crop monitoring - for hundreds of farmers across a panchayat, built for India's reality of small, fragmented landholdings.

Five stories, one thread: a reformer who gave up the comfort of tradition, a founder who built on top of an earlier setback, a woman who turned a loss of sight into sight restored for hundreds of others, a scholar who went looking for what was missing instead of assuming he knew, and a national plan built on sharing instead of owning. Nothing here scaled by adding more. It scaled by giving something up first.

coverHeadlines: Most Indian farmers can't afford their own drone. So the government's plan skips ownership entirely - and shares it instead.
September 26, 1820: born into scarcity, he became 'the Ocean of Learning' - then used it to fight his own caste.
A medical mistake took her sight as an infant. She spent her life giving 200 other blind people their independence back.
An Indian fintech founder now runs the app 3 billion people use to talk to each other.
He wanted to know why India's small-town councils keep underperforming. The answer won him one of political science's most prestigious awards.
